Simulated Annealing With an Adaptive Step

Source: R/annealing.R
sa.Rd

Creates an optimizer for a global search that accepts uphill moves with a probability that falls as the run cools, with one step length per coordinate that is adjusted during the run to hold the acceptance rate of that coordinate near a target.

Usage

sa(
  criterion = crit_stationary(),
  visiting = c("uniform", "cauchy"),
  t0 = NULL,
  cooling = 0.85,
  cycles = 3,
  steps = 10,
  step = 1,
  target_accept = 0.5,
  adjust = 2,
  n_eps = 4,
  maxit = 100,
  max_eval = Inf,
  verbose = FALSE,
  refresh = 10,
  keep_trace = FALSE
)

Arguments

criterion

The stopping rule, a criterion() object. Defaults to crit_stationary(1e-8), read on Corana's measure above. A rule that reads a gradient is rejected when the run starts, because this method computes none.

visiting

"uniform" (default) or "cauchy". Partial matching applies, and any other string is rejected by match.arg().

t0

The initial temperature, a single positive number, or NULL (the default) to calibrate it from the objective at a cost of max(10, 10 * length(par)) evaluations.

cooling

The factor by which the temperature is multiplied at each level, a single number strictly inside \((0, 1)\). Defaults to 0.85. The value 1 would never cool and 0 would freeze at once, so both endpoints are rejected.

cycles

How many step-adjustment cycles per temperature level, a positive whole number. Defaults to 3.

steps

How many sweeps of every coordinate per cycle, a positive whole number. Defaults to 10. One temperature level therefore costs cycles * steps * length(par) evaluations, and a whole run costs that times maxit, plus one for the starting value and max(10, 10 * length(par)) more if the temperature is calibrated.

step

The initial step: the step of coordinate \(j\) is step times the larger of 1 and the absolute value of that coordinate of the starting value. Defaults to 1. The adaptation changes the step of each coordinate within the first few cycles.

target_accept

The target acceptance rate of the adaptation, held inside a band of 0.1 on either side. A single number strictly inside \((0.1, 0.9)\); a value outside is rejected, because the band around it would reach 0 or 1. Defaults to 0.5.

adjust

How strongly the step is moved towards that rate, a single positive number. Defaults to 2, which is Corana's constant.

n_eps

How many temperature levels the stationarity measure covers, a positive whole number. Defaults to 4.

maxit

Maximum temperature levels. Defaults to 100. The number of levels sets how close to the minimizer the run finishes, because the step adaptation shrinks the proposal as the acceptance rate falls with the temperature.

max_eval

Maximum objective evaluations. Defaults to Inf.

verbose

Report progress? Defaults to FALSE.

refresh

Report every this many levels. Defaults to 10.

keep_trace

Store the path? Defaults to FALSE. The value column is the best so far.

Value

An S7 object of class Sa, inheriting from optimizer(), to be handed to minimize().

Details

The method is intended for problems on which a local method depends on its start: a multimodal objective, on which the answer depends on the basin in which the run begins. On a smooth problem bfgs() and newton() need far fewer evaluations, and the intended use is to pass the result of this method to one of them; see chain().

The adaptive step

The parameters are moved one coordinate at a time, and after every steps sweeps the step of each coordinate is multiplied or divided according to how often its moves were accepted, so that the rate is held inside a band around target_accept (Corana et al. 1987). The adaptation makes the method usable on a statistical objective, whose unconstrained coordinates lie on scales orders of magnitude apart, so that no single step length suits all of them. A coordinate whose moves are almost all accepted has a step that is too short to explore, and a coordinate whose moves are almost all rejected has a step that is too long.

The proposal

"uniform" draws the move uniformly on the current step of the coordinate, which together with the adaptation above is Corana's algorithm. "cauchy" draws it from a Cauchy distribution, whose heavy tail lets a run leave a basin in one move. This is the visiting distribution of fast simulated annealing (Szu and Hartley 1987), the \(q = 2\) member of the Tsallis family; the temperature still cools geometrically, as for the uniform proposal.

On a surface with many basins the Cauchy proposal reaches low values more often than the uniform one; the examples compare the two on the Rastrigin function. The default is nevertheless "uniform", which is Corana's algorithm as published and the better-behaved proposal where the objective is defined on a bounded region.

The general Tsallis visiting distribution at arbitrary \(q\) is not implemented; only the uniform and the Cauchy proposals are.

The temperature

With t0 = NULL the initial temperature is calibrated from the variation of the objective: the method samples max(10, 10 * p) proposals around the starting value, where \(p\) is the number of parameters, averages the absolute change of the objective over them, and sets \(T_0\) so that a change of that average size is accepted with probability 0.8. The calibration costs those evaluations once, before the run begins.

A fixed temperature does not suit every objective, because the Metropolis probability \(\exp(-\Delta f / T)\) compares the temperature with the scale of the objective. At \(T = 1\) a step that raises the objective by \(10^{-6}\) is accepted with probability close to 1 and the run is a random walk; one that raises it by \(10^{6}\) is accepted with probability close to 0, and the method is a local search. For an objective of small scale, such as \(10^{-6}\sum(x - (1,2))^2\), a calibrated temperature therefore gets closer to the minimizer than t0 = 1.

On a convex objective a low temperature is not a handicap, since there is a single basin, and the calibration can leave the run further from the minimizer than a fixed t0 = 1 within the same budget.

The value returned and the meaning of convergence

The result is the best point seen, not the last one, since the last point of an annealing run is a random draw from the walk. The value column of the trace is correspondingly the best value so far, and is monotone non-increasing.

The end of the schedule does not mean convergence. The stationarity measure is Corana's termination rule. At the end of each temperature level it is the largest absolute difference between the value at which the walk stopped and each of two references: the best value found so far, and the values at which the walk stopped at the last n_eps levels. It is infinite until n_eps + 1 levels have run, and crit_stationary() reads it. A run that exhausts maxit reports converged = FALSE, which for a global search is the ordinary outcome.

The run is stochastic, so set.seed() governs it, and the state from which it began is recorded in the seed of the result, so that it can be repeated.

References

Corana, A., Marchesi, M., Martini, C. and Ridella, S. (1987). Minimizing multimodal functions of continuous variables with the simulated annealing algorithm. ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software 13, 262–280.

Kirkpatrick, S., Gelatt, C. D. and Vecchi, M. P. (1983). Optimization by simulated annealing. Science 220, 671–680.

Szu, H. and Hartley, R. (1987). Fast simulated annealing. Physics Letters A 122, 157–162.

See also

chain() for handing the answer to a local method, multistart() for the other way of covering several basins, crit_stationary() for the rule that reads the measure of this method.

Examples

sa()
#> <optimizer> simulated annealing (uniform)
#>   stop when : stationarity < 1e-08
#>   budgets   : maxit 100, evaluations Inf
#>   settings  : visiting = uniform, t0 = <NULL>, cooling = 0.85, cycles = 3, steps = 10, step = 1, target_accept = 0.5, adjust = 2, n_eps = 4

# Rastrigin has many local minima (121 in the box [-5.12, 5.12]^2). A
# local method stops in the basin in which it started; this one leaves it.
rastrigin <- function(p) 10 * length(p) + sum(p^2 - 10 * cos(2 * pi * p))
set.seed(1)
minimize(sa(), rastrigin, c(4.4, -3.6))@value    # 0.914
#> [1] 0.9141033
minimize(bfgs(), rastrigin, c(4.4, -3.6))@value  # 7.96
#> [1] 7.959662

# The heavy-tailed proposal leaves a basin in one move, and on this surface
# that gives a value about two orders of magnitude lower.
set.seed(2)
minimize(sa(visiting = "cauchy", maxit = 40), rastrigin, c(4.4, -3.6))@value
#> [1] 0.002005912
set.seed(2)
minimize(sa(visiting = "uniform", maxit = 40), rastrigin, c(4.4, -3.6))@value
#> [1] 0.5458509

# The reported value is the best seen, and the trace records the same:
# it never rises, though the walk itself does.
set.seed(5)
r <- minimize(sa(maxit = 30, keep_trace = TRUE), rastrigin, c(4.4, -3.6))
all(diff(r@trace$value) <= 0)
#> [1] TRUE
all.equal(r@value, min(r@trace$value))
#> [1] TRUE

# The run repeats exactly from the state it recorded.
set.seed(11)
a <- minimize(sa(maxit = 20), rastrigin, c(4.4, -3.6))
assign(".Random.seed", a@seed, globalenv())
b <- minimize(sa(maxit = 20), rastrigin, c(4.4, -3.6))
identical(a@par, b@par)
#> [1] TRUE

# A gradient rule is rejected when the run starts, since this method
# computes no gradient.
try(minimize(sa(criterion = crit_grad()), rastrigin, c(4.4, -3.6)))
#> Error : The stopping rule needs gradient, which simulated annealing (uniform) does not provide.
#>   Choose a criterion that this optimizer can evaluate, or a method that provides it.
